summary.text: Exponentiation raises a base to an exponent, which is usually written as a small raised number to the right of the base, and the result is also called a power.
Squared and cubed get their names from geometry: b² = b · b is the area of a square with side b, and b³ = b · b · b is the volume of a cube with side b.
Powers of 10 write large or small numbers in scientific notation, and powers 2ⁿ give the number of values an n-bit binary number can take.

facts.label: Other names
facts.value: The exponent is also called the power, or the index in British English

facts.label: Scientific notation
facts.value: Base-ten powers denote large or small numbers

facts.label: Power sets
facts.value: A set with n members has a power set of 2ⁿ members

facts.label: One byte

items.prompt: A storage box has a length, width and height that are all 4 metres. Multiplying 4 by itself three times gives what property of the box?

options.label: The area of its floor
The total length of its edges
The space it takes up
The area of one wall

items.explain: Multiplying a side length by itself three times gives the volume of a cube, which is why it is called cubed.

items.prompt: A calculator is asked for zero raised to a negative power and refuses to answer. What is the reason?

options.label: It amounts to dividing by zero, which is typically undefined
Negative powers are never allowed for any base
Zero times itself is not a number the machine can store
The answer is always 1 so no calculation is needed

items.explain: Raising 0 to a negative exponent is related to division by zero, so it is typically undefined.

items.prompt: A student reasons that 2 times 3 equals 3 times 2, so swapping a base and its exponent must give the same result. What is wrong with that?

options.label: Nothing, since swapping never changes a power
Swapping only works when the exponent is even
Swapping only works when the base is ten
Unlike multiplication, a power changes when the two swap

items.explain: Exponentiation is not commutative: 2³ = 8, but reversing the operands gives the different value 3² = 9.

items.prompt: A tower of three numbers is written in superscripts with no brackets. In what order does the usual convention evaluate it?

options.label: From the bottom up, taking the lowest pair first
From the top down, taking the highest pair first
Whichever order the reader prefers
Both orders always give the same value

items.explain: Serial exponentiation is conventionally top-down (right-associative), so 2^(3²) = 2⁹ = 512, not (2³)² = 64.

items.prompt: An astronomer wants a compact way to write a distance with many zeros. Which tool from exponentiation is built for this?

options.label: Power sets of the distance
Powers of negative one
Powers of ten in scientific notation
The British word index

items.explain: Exponentiation with base 10 is used in scientific notation to denote large or small numbers.

items.prompt: A byte is an 8-bit binary number. How many different values can it take?
items.explain: An n-bit binary number can take 2ⁿ different values, and a byte may take 2⁸ = 256.

paragraphs.heading: Base and exponent
paragraphs.text: Exponentiation is an operation on two numbers, a base b and an exponent n, usually written bⁿ with the exponent raised to the right of the base. When n is a positive integer, bⁿ means multiplying b by itself n times. The exponent is also called the power, or the index in British English, and the result is also called a power. You read bⁿ as "b to the power n" or, most briefly, "b to the n".

paragraphs.heading: Squares and cubes
paragraphs.text: Two powers take their names from geometry. The expression b² is called "b squared" because a square whose sides have length b has area b². Likewise b³ is "b cubed" because a cube with side length b has volume b³.

paragraphs.heading: The rules
paragraphs.text: Multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents: bᵐ⁺ⁿ = bᵐ⋅bⁿ. Raising a power to another power multiplies the exponents: (bᵐ)ⁿ = bᵐⁿ. A number to the power 0 is generally defined to be 1, which keeps the adding rule working when one exponent is 0. Negative exponents give reciprocals, b⁻ⁿ = 1/bⁿ for nonzero b, and this is the only definition that lets the adding rule extend to negative exponents.

paragraphs.heading: Order matters
paragraphs.text: Unlike addition and multiplication, exponentiation is not commutative: 2³ = 8, but swapping the numbers gives 3² = 9. It is not associative either: (2³)² = 8² = 64, while 2^((3²)) = 2⁹ = 512. When exponents are stacked without brackets, the usual convention is to work from the top down.

paragraphs.heading: Powers of 10
paragraphs.text: In the decimal system, an integer power of 10 is written as a 1 with zeros placed according to the exponent, as in 10³ = 1000 and 10⁻⁴ = 0.0001. Scientific notation uses powers of 10 to write very large or very small numbers. The speed of light, 299792458 m/s, can be written 2.99792458×10⁸ m/s and rounded to 2.998×10⁸ m/s. Metric prefixes work the same way: the prefix kilo- stands for 10³ = 1000, which makes one kilometre equal to 1000 m.
